summary: This unit teaches you to make sure that what a business sells is sold well and delivered as promised: planning sales targets and forecasts, managing a sales team and its rewards, setting and monitoring service standards, matching staff, stock and delivery to demand, collecting customer feedback and handling complaints, keeping to consumer, pricing, credit and data rules, and reporting results with corrective action. It is written for supervisors and managers in Jamaican retail, distribution, service and public-facing organisations.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. A sale is only half the job: the customer must receive the right goods, on time, at the price promised, with good service and fair handling if something goes wrong. The manager joins **selling** (the front of the business) with **delivery** (stock, warehouse, transport, service and after-sales). When these two work apart, customers are promised what the business cannot deliver.
**Who it is for:** supervisors, sales and service managers, branch managers and officers in shops, distributors, utilities, banks, hotels and public-facing agencies.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Set targets from company goals, past results and the market; forecast; share targets among staff and branches.
Measure performance fairly, design rewards that do not cause harm, coach, run team meetings and manage time and routes.
Agree measurable standards and service level agreements, and track them.
Plan staff rosters, stock, vehicles and training for busy periods, and link sales forecasts to purchasing and warehouse.
Map the process from order to delivery, find delays and fix them, and make realistic promises.
Listen to customers and handle complaints
Collect feedback, log and learn from complaints, and put things right.
Apply consumer protection, pricing, tax, credit and data protection requirements in general terms, and act ethically.
Use a dashboard and a monthly report, find the causes of gaps, and take corrective action.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with scenario questions and short sums (targets, growth, conversion rates, commission, on-time rates).
A **written paper** with short answers (terms such as conversion rate, SLA, cross-selling) and longer answers on planning, monitoring and improving.
**Group practical tasks**: a quarterly sales and service delivery plan, and an analysis of a month's results with a role-played sales team meeting. Each member has a named role.

blocks.note: Work every sum twice. Percentages in sales work are always taken **from the base**: the target for a miss or beat, the visitors for a conversion rate, the total for a share.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A sales plan starts from three things: the **company's targets and goals**, **last year's results** (by product, customer, area and month), and **the market** (customers, competitors, prices, economy, seasons, the plans of the business). Only then do you set the target.

flow: Review last year's results by product, branch, customer and month
Study market trends, competitors and orders already in hand
Set the yearly target in J$ (and margin and volume if relevant)
Split it by quarter and month, using the seasonal pattern
Share it among branches and sales staff by their potential
Plan the resources: staff, stock, vehicles, budget, training
Agree how it will be monitored and reported

ul: **Target with growth**: last year's sales × (1 + growth rate). J$45,000,000 with 12% growth: 45,000,000 × 1.12 = **J$50,400,000**.
**Percentage of target achieved** = actual ÷ target × 100. A J$5,000,000 target and J$5,600,000 actual is 112%, a beat of **12%**.
**Miss**: J$8,000,000 target and J$7,200,000 actual is J$800,000 short, or **10%** of target.
**Growth on last year** = (this year − last year) ÷ last year.

blocks.p: Do not divide a team target equally by number of people. Base each person's share on the **potential of the area or accounts** and on **experience**. A new representative with a small area should have a lower target than an experienced one with large accounts, or the targets will not be believed or met.

A **forecast** is an estimate of future sales. The best information for next quarter is **past sales for the same season, orders already in hand, and trends**, adjusted for known changes such as a price change, a new competitor, a promotion or a holiday. Update it regularly. Share it with purchasing, the warehouse and finance so that **enough stock, staff and vehicles are ready for the expected sales**.
The **sales pipeline** shows all current opportunities by stage, from first contact to close.

flow: Lead (a possible customer)
Contact and qualify (does the person have the need, money and authority?)
Find out the customer's needs
Proposal or quotation
Negotiation
Close (won or lost)
Delivery and follow-up

blocks.p: The stage just before a written proposal is **finding out the customer's needs and qualifying the lead**. Give each stage a probability and work out the **weighted value** of the pipeline: value × probability. A J$4,000,000 deal rated 25% likely is worth J$1,000,000 in the weighted pipeline. A J$2,000,000 deal at 50% plus a J$3,000,000 deal at 20% is 1,000,000 + 600,000 = **J$1,600,000**.

No single number tells you how good a representative is. The fairest view uses **several measures**: sales against target, **margin** (not only volume), new accounts won, repeat business, conversion rate, average sale value, complaints and returns, customer feedback, and activity such as visits or calls. Compare like with like: area, product, experience.

head: Reward design
What can go wrong
Better design
rows: Pay only on the **value of sales**
Staff push unsuitable products, promise delivery they cannot keep, give large discounts and ignore after-sales
Include margin, repeat business, customer satisfaction and low complaints/returns in the reward
Bonus only for beating the team target
One weak area may be unfair; staff may stop helping each other
Reasonable rates with a quality gate

blocks.p: **Commission example:** 5% on sales above J$1,000,000 in a month. Sales of J$1,600,000 earn 5% × 600,000 = J$30,000. A representative who earns 4% above J$800,000 on sales of J$1,300,000 earns 4% × 500,000 = J$20,000.

Set **clear limits on the discounts each level of staff may give**, to protect margins and keep pricing fair and controlled. A large discount needs a manager's approval and a reason. Track discounts in the weekly report.

blocks.h: Selling honestly and for the customer

blocks.p: Good selling finds the customer's **needs** first: ask, listen, then offer what suits. If a customer wants a basic laptop for e-mail, do not push the most costly model. **Upselling** offers a higher-priced or upgraded version of what the customer came for; **cross-selling** offers related items (a case and screen guard with a new phone). Both are right only when they help the customer.

ul: **Coach**: observe, give specific feedback, agree one thing to improve. A representative who talks a lot but asks few questions needs coaching in asking questions and listening to needs.
**Product knowledge**: if staff cannot answer questions about a new range, arrange product training and simple fact sheets.
**Weekly team meeting**: review results, share leads and agree next actions. Keep it short; record actions, owners and dates.
**Recognise** good work in public; deal with problems in private.

blocks.p: Representatives who drive between shops lose selling time. **Plan routes so nearby shops are visited on the same days**, group visits by area, use phone or online contact for small accounts, and keep records so the next visit starts where the last ended.

Record every customer contact in the **CRM** system so that the team can **follow up, see the history and avoid repeat calls**. Records must be accurate, secure and used only for business. A representative must not take printouts of all customer accounts home: use the secure system, as the data policy requires.

blocks.note: Never use a reward system that makes your staff choose between a sale and the truth. Complaints rise when staff are paid only for sales.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Service standards and service level agreements

blocks.p: A **service standard** is a stated, **measurable** level of service staff must meet, for example 'answer 80% of calls within 30 seconds', 'reply to e-mails within one working day', 'deliver within 48 hours'. A **service level agreement (SLA)** is a written agreement that sets the level of service a supplier will give a customer.

flow: Find out what customers expect (complaints, surveys, call records) and what the business can deliver
Agree a few clear, measurable standards with the team
Put them in writing and explain why they matter
Give staff the tools, training and authority to meet them
Measure daily or weekly and show results
Review with the team and fix the causes when standards are missed

head: Measure
How worked out
Example
rows: Compare the rate with the promise
Promise: 98% within 48 hours. 970 of 1,000 on time is 97%: the promise was **not** kept.
Averages ten days when customers want five
Customer calls answered in 40 seconds on average
Queries solved on the first call ÷ queries
60 complaints in a month, 40 about late delivery in St Thomas

blocks.h: Order to delivery: a joined-up process

flow: Take the order accurately (product, quantity, price, address, date)
Check stock and credit
Pick, pack and check the order
Invoice
Dispatch and deliver
Confirm receipt and follow up

blocks.p: When orders arrive **incomplete** or **late**, do not just blame the warehouse or the driver. First check **how orders pass from sales to the warehouse and how stock is checked**. **Map each step of the process** with times, to find where delays happen. Common causes: sales promise what stock or transport cannot meet; orders re-keyed with mistakes; no live stock information; poor packing checks.

blocks.note: If sales staff keep promising delivery in two days but the delivery team needs five, **agree a realistic delivery time and give it to the sales staff**. A promise that cannot be kept is worse than a longer promise that is.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Use **last year's figures by day, hour and department** to find peaks (for example Friday evening and Saturday morning at a supermarket, back-to-school weeks, Christmas).
**Roster more staff for the busiest times**, plan leave early, and use part-time or temporary staff.
Book **extra vehicles, drivers and stock in advance** when sales are forecast to rise by a third at Christmas.
Share the forecast with purchasing and the warehouse so that supplies arrive before they are needed.
Train temporary staff before the peak, not during it.

blocks.p: Selling goods that are not in stock, or ordering stock the sales team cannot sell, both cost money. Hold regular meetings between sales, purchasing and the warehouse, and share the forecast and promotions calendar.

head: Method
Gives you
Watch out for
rows: Short survey by text message or tablet at the till (after the purchase)
The quickest feedback while the experience is fresh
Keep it to a few questions; low response rates
Telephone call after delivery (a car dealer calling a week after handover)
To check satisfaction and deal with concerns early
Do not turn it into a sales call
Complaints and compliments logged in one place
All channels: counter, phone, e-mail, social media
A trained person who poses as a customer and reports on the service
May reflect only the most vocal customers

blocks.p: **Satisfaction rate** = satisfied replies ÷ total replies × 100. If 150 of 200 customers rate service 4 or 5 out of 5, 75% are satisfied. **Response rate** = replies ÷ people asked.

flow: Listen without interrupting and thank the customer for telling you
Apologise for the experience and take ownership
Find the facts and check the record, policy and the customer's rights
Offer a fair solution, or explain clearly what cannot be done and why
Act, and tell the customer when it is done
Log the complaint and its cause, and look for a pattern

blocks.p: When a major customer threatens to cancel after three wrong orders, the sales manager should **contact the customer promptly, own the problem and agree a fix with dates**, then follow up. A problem fixed well can raise loyalty.
Use complaint data to **fix the process**, not just the case. If 40 of 60 complaints are about late deliveries in one parish, find the cause of the delays and fix it.

ul: A **warranty** is the maker's or seller's promise to repair or replace faulty goods within a stated period. If a refrigerator fails within warranty, arrange repair or replacement under the terms.
Make **returns policy** clear, in writing, at the till and online.
Keep spare parts, repair partners and response times in the plan.
Call new buyers to check they are satisfied and to deal with concerns early.

blocks.note: Customers who complain and are treated well often return. Customers who are ignored often say nothing and leave. Look for the silent ones through surveys and follow-up calls.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Goods and services must **match their description**, be of **fit quality** and do what they are sold for.
Sellers must not mislead customers about **price, quality or terms**.
Prices should be **clearly shown and charged correctly**. If a shelf label and till disagree, follow the pricing policy, which usually honours the label shown to the customer, and correct the system.
Returns, refunds and warranties must follow the policy and the customer's rights under the law.

blocks.p: Refer to the rules by their purpose (consumer protection) and to the business's own policy. This unit does not ask for section numbers.

Issue proper **receipts** showing **GCT** where it applies, at the rate that applies at the time. Keep records for the period required. At the point of sale, correct receipts and recorded sales help the business meet its tax duties.

Before a large order is delivered to a customer whose account is badly overdue, **check with credit control and follow the credit policy**. Sales staff should not release goods on their own authority. Credit control and sales should agree limits, terms and who may approve exceptions.

Customer lists, phone numbers and purchase histories are **personal data**. The general aims of the data protection law are to collect only what is needed, use it for the stated purpose, keep it accurate and secure, and keep it no longer than necessary. Use the secure system, not private copies.

A business that starts taking orders online must have in place **clear prices, secure payment, order handling and delivery times** before the service goes live. Test it, train staff, and make sure that stock and delivery capacity match the online promise.

ul: Do not make false promises or false claims.
Declare gifts and conflicts of interest under the policy.
Treat customers fairly whatever their size.
Do not pressure staff into misleading customers.

blocks.p: A **sales dashboard** drawing on the **point-of-sale system** lets the manager see each day how sales compare with targets across all branches. Show a few key measures: sales against target, margin, conversion rate, average sale value, stock availability, on-time delivery, complaints and satisfaction. Update daily or weekly, show trends and use RAG colours.

blocks.h: When a team misses its target

flow: Analyse the figures by product, area, person and week to find where the gap is
Check the causes: stock, price, competitors, staff, promotion, service problems, data errors
Talk to the team and customers
Decide actions with owners and dates
Review progress at the next meeting

blocks.p: If a team misses its target two months in a row, **analyse the figures to find the cause before deciding on a remedy**. Do not just push harder, or change the target, or blame a person.

blocks.h: The monthly report to senior management

ul: **Results against target** (sales, margin, key measures)
**Reasons for gaps**, in plain words
**Planned actions**, with owners and dates
Service results: on-time rate, complaints, satisfaction
Risks and resource needs
One page of summary, with tables behind it
Fix the process that causes repeated complaints.
Use training for gaps in skill and product knowledge.
Share what the best performers do.
Review targets and standards each quarter against results.
Recognise improvement.

blocks.p: A branch had a sales target of J$6,000,000 and sold J$5,400,000 from 900 sales. Visitors were 3,600. Of 1,000 deliveries, 950 were on time. Of 120 survey replies, 90 were satisfied.

ul: Sales against target: 5,400,000 ÷ 6,000,000 = 90%, a **10% miss** (J$600,000 short).
Conversion rate = 900 ÷ 3,600 = **25%**.
On-time delivery = 950 ÷ 1,000 = **95%**.
Satisfaction = 90 ÷ 120 = **75%**.

blocks.p: To find the cause of the miss, compare conversion and average sale against last month and against other branches. If conversion is normal but visitors fell, the cause is traffic, such as weather or marketing; if visitors are normal but conversion fell, look at stock and service on the floor.

blocks.note: A figure is only useful if you ask 'compared with what?' and 'why?'.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: start a sales plan from targets, past results and the market, and work out a target with growth
share a team target fairly and forecast with seasonal data and orders in hand
work out the weighted value of a pipeline, conversion rate, average sale value and commission
judge a representative by several measures and design rewards that do not harm service
control discounts and coach staff in needs-based selling
set measurable service standards and an SLA, and check promises against results
work out on-time delivery rates and find delays by mapping the order-to-delivery process
plan staff, stock and vehicles for busy periods and share forecasts with purchasing and the warehouse
collect customer feedback, handle a complaint and use complaint data to improve
apply consumer protection, pricing, tax, credit and data protection requirements in general terms
use a dashboard and write a monthly report with causes and actions
take corrective action when targets or standards are missed

terms: The sales goal for a period / an estimate of future sales.
All current sales opportunities, by stage.
Deal value × chance of closing, added up.
The share of visitors or leads who buy.
Selling a higher version / selling related items.
A stated, measurable level of service.
Service level agreement: a written agreement on service levels.
The time from order to delivery.
On-time deliveries as a percentage of all deliveries.
A person who poses as a customer to assess service.
Customer relationship management: the system that records customer contacts.
The till system that records sales, payments and stock.
A promise to repair or replace faulty goods within a period.
Set wording a telephone sales team follows.

c1.title: Mandeville school-supplies distributor
c1.text: A distributor of school supplies in Mandeville sold J$45,000,000 last year, with about half of it in July to September for the back-to-school season. The sales manager, Ms Hyacinth Brown, wants 12% growth this year and has four representatives: one very experienced with large school accounts, one with a medium area, and two new ones with small areas. Her pipeline holds three deals: J$3,000,000 rated 60% likely, J$2,500,000 rated 40% likely and J$4,000,000 rated 10% likely.

c2.title: Kingston tyre and battery shop
c2.text: A tyre and battery shop in Kingston pays its sales staff only on the value of sales. Over six months, sales have grown but margin has fallen, returns have risen and customers complain that fitting dates were not kept. One representative, Orville, made 92 sales worth J$2,300,000 against a target of J$2,000,000, but gave large discounts. The proposed new scheme pays 3% commission on monthly sales above J$1,500,000, and adds measures for margin and complaints.

c3.title: Port Antonio gas-cylinder delivery
c3.text: A firm in Port Antonio delivers gas cylinders to households and restaurants in Portland and St Thomas. It promises delivery within 48 hours on 95% of orders. Last month it made 600 deliveries, and 552 were on time. Most late deliveries were orders taken after 2 p.m., which reach the warehouse the next morning. Sales staff do not see stock levels, so some orders are accepted when cylinders are not available. Demand is expected to rise by a third before Christmas.

c4.title: Ocho Rios electronics retailer
c4.text: An electronics retailer in Ocho Rios sends a text survey after each sale. Last month 250 customers replied; 190 rated their experience 4 or 5 out of 5. The complaints log shows a pattern: customers buy televisions, then learn that wall-mounting is not included; a customer returned a television that stopped working two weeks after purchase, within the warranty, and was told to wait for the manager. The owner is considering hiring a mystery shopper.

c5.title: Christiana farm-supplies branch
c5.text: A farm-supplies business in Christiana has a customer account that is J$700,000 overdue. The farmer, a long-time customer, wants a large fertiliser order delivered tomorrow. The sales representative has promised it. The branch manager, Mr Andrew Palmer, must send a monthly report to head office. He also finds a representative has copied the customer list, with phone numbers and credit balances, to a personal phone.

questions.q: What is Ms Brown's sales target for this year?
o: J$45,000,012, found by adding the 12 growth points to last year's total
J$57,000,000, found by adding J$12,000,000 to last year's sales
J$46,200,000, found by multiplying last year's sales by 1.12 only for half of the year
questions.why: J$45,000,000 × 1.12 = J$50,400,000. Growth is a percentage of last year's figure and is added to it. Check: 12% of 45,000,000 is 5,400,000, and 45,000,000 + 5,400,000 = 50,400,000.

questions.q: What is the weighted value of Ms Brown's pipeline?
o: J$9,500,000, the total value of the three deals if all of them were won
J$2,000,000, the value of the deal with the highest chance of closing
J$1,900,000, found by taking an average of the three percentages times the largest deal

questions.q: How should she share the target among the four representatives?
o: Equally, at J$12,600,000 each, so that nobody can say the shares are unfair
By who sold the most last year, so that the best sellers carry the load
With the new representatives taking the largest share, so that they learn faster
By each area's potential and the representative's experience
questions.why: Equal shares ignore the size of each area. Targets based on potential and experience are seen as fair and are more likely to be achieved, and they can be adjusted as the year goes on.

questions.q: Half of last year's sales fell in July to September. What does this mean for her plan?
o: Divide the target equally across the twelve months, to keep the monthly figures simple
Plan stock and staff for the average month and rely on overtime in the peak
Phase the target by month and plan staff, stock and vehicles for the peak
Move the peak by offering discounts in the first half of the year
questions.why: Seasonal sales mean the target and resources must follow the pattern. Share the forecast with purchasing and the warehouse so that stock arrives before the peak.

questions.q: Orville made 92 sales worth J$2,300,000. What was his average sale value, and by what percentage did he beat his target?
o: J$25,000, and a beat of 13%, found by dividing the J$300,000 by the J$2,300,000
J$22,000, and a beat of 15%, found by using 100 sales instead of 92
J$25,000, and a beat of 15%
J$2,300, and a beat of 30%, found by dividing the J$300,000 by 1,000

questions.q: Under the new scheme, how much commission does Orville earn if his J$2,300,000 was sold in one month?
o: J$69,000, since 3% is paid on the whole of J$2,300,000
J$9,000, since 3% is paid only on the J$300,000 above his target
J$45,000, since 3% is paid on the J$1,500,000 threshold
questions.why: 3% of the amount above J$1,500,000: 800,000 × 3% = J$24,000. The rate applies only to the portion above the threshold.

questions.q: Why does the shop's present pay scheme cause rising returns and complaints?
o: Pay is based only on sales value, so staff may oversell, discount heavily and ignore service
Staff are paid too little in basic salary, so they do not care about the shop's good reputation
The shop's customers expect lower prices than staff are allowed to give them on tyres
Targets are shared equally among all staff, so the weaker sellers become discouraged and leave
questions.why: A reward on sales value alone says that nothing else matters. Staff may push unsuitable products or promise what cannot be done. Adding margin, repeat business, complaints and returns balances it.

questions.q: Which control best protects the shop's margin from heavy discounting?
o: Ban all discounts so that every customer pays the list price, whatever the competition does
Let staff discount freely to win sales and review the margin once a year at the year end
Pay staff a higher rate of commission on discounted sales to reward them for winning customers
Set discount limits for each level of staff, with manager approval above them
questions.why: Clear discount limits protect margins and keep pricing fair. A ban is unrealistic, and no control or a reward for discounting encourages the problem.

questions.q: What was the on-time rate, and did the firm keep its promise?
o: 92%, and yes, because most orders were delivered on time
8%, and no, because only a small share of orders were late
95%, and yes, because the firm has promised 95%
92%, and no, because it is below the promised 95%
questions.why: 552 ÷ 600 = 92%. The promise was 95%, so the firm needed at least 570 on time. It was 18 deliveries short, so it did not keep the promise.

questions.q: Most late deliveries are for orders taken after 2 p.m. What is the best first step?
o: Tell the drivers to work faster and to take shorter breaks on orders taken in the afternoon
Stop taking orders after 2 p.m. until the warehouse has taken on more staff for the evening
Map the order-to-delivery steps to see where afternoon orders wait, then redesign the cut-off
Offer discounts on afternoon orders as an apology to customers for each late delivery
questions.why: Mapping the process shows where time is lost: here, orders reach the warehouse the next morning. Fix the cause (for example, a later pick-up time or a realistic promise), not the symptom.

questions.q: Sales staff accept orders when cylinders are not in stock. What should the manager change?
o: Warn customers that orders are not guaranteed, after they have paid
Give sales staff live stock information and realistic delivery dates
Ask the warehouse to keep a very large stock of every cylinder size
Stop giving delivery dates to customers
questions.why: Sales and delivery must work as one system. Live stock information lets staff promise what the business can deliver. Excess stock is costly and no dates would harm customers.

questions.q: Demand is expected to rise by a third before Christmas. Which plan matters most?
o: Book extra vehicles, drivers and cylinders ahead, and share the forecast with the warehouse
Wait to see how many orders arrive and then hire extra drivers once delays begin to appear
Rely on the current staff working longer hours in the peak weeks of the Christmas season
Raise delivery prices sharply before Christmas to reduce the number of orders received
questions.why: A third more orders needs more resources booked early. Responding after delays begin means customers have already been let down.

questions.q: What share of customers who replied were satisfied?
questions.why: 190 ÷ 250 = 0.76 = 76%. The total replies (250) are the base. Check: 76% of 250 = 190.

questions.q: How should the shop handle the customer whose television failed within the warranty?
o: Ask for the receipt again, and offer a discount on a new television to settle the matter
Refer the customer to the manufacturer and take no further action on the complaint
Refuse the claim until the manager decides, whatever the warranty terms may say
Arrange repair or replacement under the warranty, and apologise for the wait
questions.why: Goods that fail within warranty should be repaired or replaced as the terms say, promptly. Sending customers away, or delaying, damages trust and may breach their rights.

questions.q: The complaints log shows many customers surprised that wall-mounting is not included. What is the right response?
o: Reduce the number of televisions on display, so fewer customers expect wall-mounting
Refund every customer who complains about wall-mounting, whatever the shop's sales terms say
Explain what is and is not included at the point of sale, and train staff to do so
Ask customers to stop making complaints about the shop on social media and send them to the owner
questions.why: The complaint pattern shows a gap in information at the sale. Fix the process: clear explanation, a note on the price tag and training. Otherwise the same complaint will repeat.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the mystery shopper the owner is considering?
o: To catch individual staff out and so justify dismissal for poor service
To report on the real service a customer receives, against agreed criteria
To replace customer surveys and the records of complaints with one expert report
To increase sales by pretending to be a customer and placing large orders
questions.why: A mystery shopper gives an independent view of the service, which is then used to coach staff and improve standards. It adds to, and does not replace, survey and complaints data.

questions.q: The farmer's account is J$700,000 overdue and the rep has promised delivery. What should Mr Palmer do?
o: Deliver the order, since the farmer is a long-time customer and has been promised
Check with credit control and follow the credit policy before any delivery
Cancel the order and tell the farmer never to order again
Deliver half of the order and send a bill for the rest
questions.why: Releasing goods to an account that is badly overdue needs credit control's decision under the policy. Sales and credit should agree an arrangement, and the rep should not have promised delivery.

questions.q: What should Mr Palmer say about the representative copying the customer list to a personal phone?
o: It is not allowed: have it removed, use only the secure system, and apply the data policy
It is fine as long as the phone has a password and nobody else uses the phone
It is allowed when the representative needs to work after hours or at weekends
It is acceptable if the credit balances are removed and only the phone numbers stay
questions.why: Personal data must be kept secure and used for the stated purpose. Copies on personal devices are a breach of the data policy, and the manager must act on it.

questions.q: What should Mr Palmer's monthly report to head office contain?
o: Only the total sales figure for the month, with the figure for the same month last year
A full list of every transaction and every customer account for the month
A summary of the staff's opinions of how the month went for the branch
Results against target, the reasons for any gaps and the actions planned
questions.why: A monthly report should show results against target, causes of gaps and planned actions, with a few key service measures. A list of figures without causes does not help decisions.

questions.q: While serving a farmer who is buying fertiliser, a representative also suggests gloves and a hand sprayer for applying it. What is this practice called?
o: Upselling, because the farmer is offered more items to buy
Discounting, because the extra items are priced separately
Cross-selling, if the items truly help the farmer
Credit selling, because the items are added to the account
questions.why: Offering related items that go with what the customer is buying is cross-selling. Upselling is offering a higher-priced version of the same item. Both are fair only when they meet a real need.
